title: Notes of Ministry - 95 - October 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 95 - October 19 (2502)/Notes of Ministry - 95 - Octobe - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: It is a very attractive subject that one desires to say a brief word about, beloved, though I feel so inadequate to expound on such a subject as friendship with God, friendship with the Lord Jesus, and friendship with the saints. It is a very attractive and marvellous matter that divine Persons should deign to call us into friendship with Themselves, and should be prepared to have communion and intimacy with creatures—wonderful grace, wonderful privilege!

I wish to say a brief word as to Abraham being a friend of God and on some of the features that qualified him to be this. For surely to be a friend of God there must be moral qualities and moral features. Then the Lord has His friends; “I call you no longer bondmen ... but I have called you friends”, John 15: 15. Friendship would involve intimacy with the Person and the knowledge of the Person. It is a wonderful joy that the Lord has with the assembly, taking the saints, His bride, into His confidence. Is not that marvellous that we should be elevated to have communion, intimacy, and friendship as the bride? It is wonderful to be part of the bride, and to be born in this dispensation. We might have been born in Old Testament times and never have had part in the bride of Christ, but in the sovereignty of God we are born in this dispensation and have the Spirit; we are part of Christ’s bride.

I would like to mention—not necessarily in their moral order—the features that qualified Abraham to be a friend of God. One would be the intimacy he had with Jehovah, another would be the confidence he had in God—a matter in which we all need furthering, to have confidence in the Father’s love and care. He loves to have our confidence, beloved. Job was sorely tried in his confidence in God; what discipline he passed through, but the devil did not win. He was allowed to discipline Job and pass him through severe trials that hardly any other person has passed through, but the devil did not get the victory. Although Job said things that were not quite right, his faith in God was there, and he came through and was blessed abundantly, I would say with the double portion.

Now Abraham was marked by intimacy, confidence, and faithfulness. Would not these be features that God would look for in those called His friends? In the Scriptures three times he is called a friend of God, a wonderful, dignified appellation. The God of glory appeared to him and he answered to the call. The God of glory has appeared to us and called us with a heavenly calling out of this world, out of kindred, house, and country, that we might belong to a heavenly country, and heavenly citizenship. We have been called by the God of glory and that must end in glory, and in the meantime we are learning to have communion with the God of glory, known to us in a special way in the name of Father—what a Father! How blessed to speak to the Father. He is a holy Father, blessed Father, and a loving Father too.

Let us have more intimacy with the Father and cultivate using our own language—He loves you to use your own language. Just speak to God as you know Him yourself, reverently, of course, with titles in keeping with the Scriptures; but He loves you to use your own language in private with Him as you go into your closet. Shut the door on everything else outside, every distraction (not so easy sometimes) and speak to the Father in secret, and the Father who sees in secret will render it to thee (see Matthew 6: 6). What a blessed God He is!

Abraham responded but was detained with his father for a while, but after that he moved forward. We are going to move forward to the rapture, maybe very soon. The God of glory has appeared to us; we have been called by a heavenly calling; never let the devil get you away from that. He would like us to be an earthly people; he would like us to descend to the earth and be earthly minded, enemies of the cross of Christ, and minding earthly things. That is searching, is it not? But Abraham answered to the call, he was obedient. Would not that be one qualification to be a friend of God?—obedience to His call, obedience to His word, and obedience to His will, whatever the cost. He left his country, his relatives, he left everything to answer to the call, to be pleasing to God, and he was thus qualifying to be a friend of God.

He had an altar and was characteristically a man of prayer. I think that to be qualified to be called God’s friend we would need to be marked characteristically by prayer, having to do with God every day. Abraham had a large household, a large number of servants, but he would constantly turn to God. He had an influence over Lot; bringing God into everything, he was able to rescue him; he interceded for Lot, as being marked by prayer.

Obedience would be another qualification—obedience, prayer, intimacy, and faithfulness. I think faithfulness would be a prime quality; whatever the cost, standing by His word, standing by the truth and divine principles. I feel I come short of these features. I am suggesting these thoughts that we may desire to qualify to be friends of God. What dignity!

Fancy a person being able to say of you, ‘He is a friend of God, one that God can confide in’. If God says, ‘I know he will command his household after him’. God had confidence in him. How weak some of us have been! When you go over things with God in private you wonder where the defect has been. You thought you were bringing your children up for the Lord and not for the world, yet when they have grown up they may have gone away. You say, Where was the defect? You are humbled before God. While in one sense it is our responsibility if they go astray, it is sovereignty if our children are brought in, but God says to Abraham, “I know him that he will command his children and his household”. God knew he would not allow worldliness or anything that was not in keeping with God’s house.

When Abraham is pleading with God about those in Sodom he says, “I, who am dust and ashes”, What humility! Would not that be a qualification, beloved? suggesting self-abnegation in the presence of God. It is a real thing to be in the presence of God in a sense of your nothingness. Dust—what is more worthless than dust?—and ashes suggests he had gone through the fire. A spiritual man would judge in himself everything that was judged at the cross. The final test was when he was told to offer up Isaac. Oh how delightful it must have been for God to see that! He was ready to obey His word even to taking up the knife to slay his son, a supreme test, but the friend of God rose to the occasion. It speaks in 2 Chronicles 20: 7 of Abraham being God’s friend and the alternative rendering is one who loves God. He loved God, so he stands out morally and spiritually as a friend of God. May we covet these features of intimacy, faithfulness, and prayer so that God may have confidence in us; He has confidence in the Saints who are faithful.

Now I want to speak a little about John 3. I think the thought of the Bridegroom and the bride is greater than anything that came out in the Old Testament. Abraham is not part of the bride, although, as we have been taught, he will be among the guests at the marriage of the Lamb. So here we have John the baptist a friend of the Bridegroom; what a friend! It says “the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices in heart because of the voice of the bridegroom”. He was near to Christ, willing to be superseded. The Lord says, “There is not arisen among the born of women a greater than John the baptist. But he who is a little one in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he”, Matthew 11: 11.

So, beloved, what a great thing it is to be in the bride. What qualified John to be a friend of Christ? Separation—he was a Nazarite to God from birth—he was in the wilderness with God; his garment was unworldly; there was nothing worldly about him at all, a man that was absolutely faithful and filled with the Holy Spirit. How the Lord appreciated him! how He felt it when John was beheaded, a man so faithful as a friend that he was prepared to be martyred. John spoke to Herod about taking the wife of his brother and he lost his life—what faithfulness! The Lord valued him.

I want to speak a little of the relationship of the Bridegroom and the bride, for John stands there saying, “Ye yourselves bear me witness that I said, I am not the Christ, but, that I am sent before him. He that has the bride is the bridegroom”. Can you be in the presence of the Bridegroom without rejoicing in Him? I do not think so. If you are in the presence of the Bridegroom it must result in joy, for it is delightful and exquisite to hear the voice of the Bridegroom, to hear the voice of Christ, for He is the lover of the assembly. He has the bride in His embrace; is that not a wonderful conception of Christ and the assembly? The bride is also the Lamb’s wife, now in the scene of suffering. We will suffer now if we are faithful to Christ, denying the flesh and the world, but nevertheless the bride exists and there is no failure with the bride because it is the work of God in the saints and there is no failure with that.

The public side of the testimony, with the candlestick, has failed, but what a wonderful thing that the Spirit and the bride say “Come” at the end of the dispensation. We are right there, beloved, and I suggest to the saints that the Lord is looking for bridal affection. He is looking for it collectively amongst us, in localities, just as Rebecca was a bride and wife to Isaac, in the absence of Sarah, in the tent. It is like the local position, espoused as a chaste virgin to Christ. So let us be marked more by bridal features—chastity, holiness, virginity, purity, separation, a moral loveliness that Christ by the Spirit has wrought in us. The Spirit is serving the brethren to form us in the features of that heavenly Man, because we are soon going to go into the wedding—the public celebration of the marriage.

What a day that will be when Babylon is overthrown with all its vain-glory, vanity, sinfulness, assumption, and idolatry, and when all that has been overthrown then comes forward the marriage of the Lamb. Christ and the assembly will fill the whole scene. The Lord will deal with all that is apostate, all that is against Him. He will deal with it with a rod of iron. He will break in pieces all the opposition of men who worship the beast and its image. We are to be intelligent and know what is going to take place, but we are not to be too much occupied with that. In spite of all the lawlessness, evil, and violence obtaining at the present time, I believe God will keep His hand on this country and preserve it from anarchy because of His people. He has thousands unknown to us who love Him. There are thousands that have not bowed the knee to. Baal nor kissed him; they may not have the light of the assembly, but He has many people in this country.

We are privileged, as having the light of the assembly, to know what the bride is and the preciousness of the bride to the Bridegroom. He loves His assembly, and He enjoys the affectionate responses of the saints, not only when we are together on Lord’s day mornings, but bridal affections characteristically marking us. We desire to be loyal to Christ our absent One. We desire to be in the hands of the Spirit, as Rebecca was typically, and be formed in those features, the adornment that was put on Rebecca and the communion she had; typically, with the Spirit. As she journeyed to the heavenly man, she would more and more get a picture of what Isaac was like. She is described as a maiden, a damsel, a virgin, a daughter; all—these things afford a beautiful picture of—the bride, and that is what the Spirit is working out.

Is it worthwhile, the exercise and a measure of suffering? Surely it makes worthwhile the suffering; the separate path; and a bit of reproach. Surely it is worth it to give this satisfaction to the Bridegroom.
It is lovely to hear His voice. John would say, ‘I do not form part of the bride, but it is grand to be near to Christ, to be in His company, to listen to His quickening voice’. We sing,

‘We’ve heard Thy quick’ning voice’ (Hymn 137). What a voice the voice of Christ is! soon we shall be hearing it without the weakness of the body and the weakness of nature. We shall be hearing it in bodies of glory, spiritual bodies that can more fully respond to Him. John qualified to be a friend of the Bridegroom and may we qualify to be friends of Christ, we who are part of the bride. He is above all; He is heavenly.

Christianity is heavenly, its origin and destiny are heaven; we are a heavenly people by calling. Let us maintain our heavenly citizenship and do not let us drop down to indulge in anything below that level, whether in reading, associations, or anything else. Let us maintain the holiness and chastity of the bride which the blessed Spirit is bent on working out in those who are available to Him. He may not have many available to Him to form in bridal features, but the Lord will credit the whole assembly with what He may find in a remnant in the way of Philadelphian features.

Now in the last scripture it is a matter of being friendly among ourselves. Friendship involves intimacy, as suggested here. John says, “I had many things to write to thee, but I will not with ink and pen ... but I hope soon to see thee, and we will speak mouth to mouth”. That is a beautiful suggestion of friendship, mouth to mouth, real intimacy and transparency, confidence, and nearness. I think the Lord would be delighted with that in our localities, to see us as brethren near to one another, transparent with one another, really friendly, with no hypocrisy; not being with the brethren in the meeting and then saying something different outside, but mouth to mouth, in intimacy. It is said that the saints in New Testament days greeted one another with a holy kiss. That suggests intimacy and friendship. How can you hold anything against a brother and yet kiss him? That would be like Judas. He kissed the Lord, and the Lord Jesus said, “Deliverest thou up the Son of man with a kiss?”, (Luke 22: 48), as much as to say, ‘Do you do this act of betrayal with what is an emblem of nearness and friendship? Do you betray me with a kiss?’ The
Lord felt it. Judas did it with what is symbolic of confidence and intimacy.

So may we greet the friends by name. It is remarkable that we now know practically all the brethren and can greet them all by name. Thus knowing them, we are concerned if one is suffering; there are body feelings; so the suggestion is of family conditions. It is a great thing to enjoy a family spirit of confidence and love where the Spirit is free, and where love is flowing. Where there is unity among the brethren the Lord can command the blessing, like the oil that flowed from Aaron’s head down to the hem of his garments (Psalm 133). We receive the blessing of the Lord as we are together in organic unity. I think “Greet the friends by name”, and seeing them and speaking mouth to mouth suggests an organic unity that is delightful to heaven. May it be so for His name’s sake.

I have been exercised recently, dear brethren, about the realization of the presence of the Lord. I am sure that we would all agree that the realization of His presence must be exceeding joy. One has been concerned not simply to have the faith of it, but to have the consciousness of it, to be assured of His presence by that means. It seems to me to be of the utmost importance that we should

be conscious of the Lord’s presence with us, peculiarly at the Supper and in the service of God. Then His presence with us in the testimony too; we may take it for granted, but I think the Lord would always raise an exercise with us as to the conditions that are suited to Him, because He obviously cannot dwell anywhere, in anybody, in any state. Now if I think of His presence in what I might call an objective way, it must be ecstasy, as it will be when we are with Him. If I place my experience alongside of that then I have to question how far I have realized it.

Perhaps we could all think that over, not with a view in any sense to our being discouraged, because when the Lord calls attention to various truths and exhorts us as to various experiences, as He is doing in these days, it is never to discourage; it is always to encourage us. So that if, for example, He raises the question with our younger brethren as to the reception of the Spirit, or with any of us as to how much room we give to the Spirit, it is not to discourage us by self-occupation but to encourage us to get to Him that we might receive the Spirit, and as giving more place to Him might be aware of His dwelling with us in unhindered conditions.

Now Moses was evidently very concerned about this for the people. Previously he had cast God back, so to speak, on His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (see Exodus 32: 13); not Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. When you come to Elijah he does the same thing, he casts God back on His promises to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (see 1 Kings 18: 36). That is to say, those two men understood, in days when the people had broken down, that God’s thoughts were centred in Israel, that is, they looked at his spiritual name rather than his name of responsibility where he had the discipline of God.

Now Moses is most urgent with God about the bringing up of the people and His presence going with them—“If thy presence do not go, bring us not up”. I think we can see the force of it, dear brethren, because Moses would understand that the wilderness was a very barren place, full of dead bodies, dead bones, and of everything that would contaminate. If a path was made in the desert it would very soon be covered by the sand and very many other things, so that the desert would become, as we used to sing, pathless; hence the need of divine guidance. The same is true today; the world, or the wilderness, to us is full of dead bodies and dead bones; a union is a dead body; that is just an example. Many other kinds of associations are but dead bodies in the wilderness, things which are contaminating, and of which the Lord has spoken to us and from which, through His grace, we are free I believe. Nevertheless, the desert insofar as the saints are concerned is pathless and apart from the presence of the Lord there is no guidance in it. Now this raises a very sobering question for us, as to how far we realize the presence of the Lord and divine guidance. I think we have it, but we need to be increasingly exercised both as individuals, in our local companies, and generally, as to the presence of God and His approval.

I believe the anointing involves the approval of God, and hence the question arises as to how far we may be in the power of that. Jesus was anointed and approved of God, as He says, “He has anointed me”, (Luke 4: 18), and He preached the glad tidings in the power of the anointing, the power of the Holy Spirit; but now for us, dear brethren, in these days when things are so broken—and I suppose there have never been days like it—it seems to me that if there is one thing of all moment that we need to consider it is the presence

and support of the Lord and that, as having some consciousness of it, we should, like Moses, be urgent with the Lord that we might be aware of His presence and so be brought into God’s purpose for us. So he says here, “And now, if indeed I have found grace in thine eyes, make me now to know thy way, that I may know thee, that I may find grace in thine eyes; and consider that this nation is thy people!”. God says, “My presence shall go, and I will give thee rest”. What a promise that is, and the promise I believe is for God’s people, but despite that fact Moses is still urgent that God should be with them; he says, “If thy presence do not go, bring us not up hence”.

It seems to me that to that man, of whom God says He knew him face to face, the presence of God meant even more than being in the promised land, because he says, “If thy presence do not go, bring us not up”, as much as to say, What would the bringing up be, what would the land be, what would all its fruitfulness be, without the presence of the blessed God? In other words, what would the blessings be without the Blesser? How often we dwell upon the blessings without reaching the Blesser and without understanding the Godward aspect of the work of Jesus which has in mind that God should be glorified and praised and blessed among His beloved people. Let us then think more of this Godward aspect of the work of Jesus and let us be even more concerned about the realization of the presence of the Lord than we may be about accurate doctrine. Thank God for the doctrine, and thank God for those we know among us who have a knowledge of the doctrine and can help us; may they continue to do so; but I believe that what is of primary importance is that we should be assured of, and realize, the presence of God.
Now, God having committed Himself in this way,

Moses says, ‘Show me Thy glory’. We know he was put in the cleft of the rock; that has been likened to the ‘in Christ Jesus’ position. That does not break down. So we are taken into favour in Him, we are all one in Christ Jesus, and it is most noticeable that in the epistles to Timothy, and particularly in the second, so much is emphasized as being “in Christ Jesus”, that is, it is beyond any breakdown; it is a rock. “His purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time” (2 Timothy 1: 9): Paul, so to speak, is establishing that young man in the cleft of the rock, the rock of God’s purpose.

We have “in Christ Jesus” in chapter 1 before he brings in the facing of all the problems and the sorrows, and the necessity to withdraw from iniquity, in chapter 2. First of all he says, so to speak, Timothy, you can rest assured that all is in the rock, “in Christ Jesus”; “be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus”; and he speaks of the “promise of life, the life which is in Christ Jesus”. Others have likened it to the cleft in the rock; that is where Moses was put.

You know, he would feel very secure there, dear brethren, would he not? I think as we sit here this morning we can be very secure and realize that we are secure because everything is immutably settled in that blessed Man at the right hand of God. Presently everything will be put into effect and we shall be with Him in the full actuality of what belongs to us; there is no doubt about that. My concern for myself and for my brethren is that we should realize, if I might use that word, the presence of the Lord increasingly among us.
Now in Matthew 18 the Lord speaks very simply. He has spoken about the assembly before this, as we know. The light of it was brought out in chapter 16 and then He speaks of it in this chapter, “tell

it to the assembly” (Matthew 5:17); we know the passage very well and I do not wish to dwell on it, but in the verses I have read He says, “Again I say to you, that if two of you shall agree on the earth concerning any matter, whatsoever it may be that they shall ask, it shall come to them from my Father who is in the heavens”. One has tried a little before to speak on this passage, and I do not think one can say anything very fresh about it, but what I find in it is very testing. It seems to me that the Lord is speaking to persons whom He credits with being committed to His testimony. Hence what they would ask would not be for personal advantage or gain; the idea or motive of ambition would not be with them; what they would ask of His Father in heaven surely would be something for the glory of Christ, and if for the glory of Christ, for the glory of the Father. He says, “it shall come to them from my Father who is it the heavens”. Are you in the faith of that? You are entitled to ask me the same thing.
Am I in the faith of that?

Any “two of you”, as we have been taught, and the context of the passage seems to make it perfectly clear, is two of the assembly, however small things may become; and if the Lord is anticipating the breakdown here, as it has been suggested He is, He says any “two of you”.

“For” or ‘because’, I judge—“where two or three are gathered together unto my name, there am I in the midst of them”. “Two or three”; we are more than that, are we not, at the present moment; most localities are more than that. I would like to emphasize the words of the Lord Jesus; I find it essential to read Scripture word by word; read it first without amplification or interpretation; read what is written first—“where two or three are gathered together unto my name, there am I in the midst of them”. “Gathered together”; it is fairly easy to be gathered without being together,

and I suppose it is fairly easy to be together without being gathered properly, I judge that when the Lord used the words “gathered together”, what He would have in His mind for days of breakdown would be assembling; He would be speaking in the light of the assembly.

You see, some of us were tested in the forces when we came into contact with various persons in various denominations who suggested that, on the basis of this verse, we should come together to read the Scriptures, and to pray, and maybe if thought appropriate to break bread. That suggestion was not too easy to meet, as you can imagine. Maybe most of us now who are much older would be able to meet it more easily, but when we were young men it was not so easy. Why not? “Two or three”; we will come together, and the Lord will be with us; but I believe the Lord has deliberately, and skilfully, included the words “gathered together”, and I fail to see, as we were then helped to see, how persons who belong to different groups of believers who are alienated from one another could possibly be considered as being “gathered together”; both words are needed, and I think the ground we need to be on, dear brethren, is being “gathered together”. I believe, as I have said, that in anticipating days of breakdown, the Lord uses the words “gathered together”, as much as to say, Well, you can come together in the light of the assembly, but if you are to have the functioning of the assembly you must have assembly formation.

That is what the Lord is doing at the present moment in the service of the ministry, a ministry that is reaching us, and, thank God, is reaching many others in printed form. It has in mind that there should be a reception of the truth, and a readiness to be governed by the truth, that there should be assembly formation and assembly function.

I believe these verses in a general way would have that in mind. It is not, as we know, the Supper but seems to be more general as to those gathered together. And He adds, “there am I in the midst of them”. Now I wonder if we have experienced this, whether we are aware of it.

I believe it to be true; that is quite obvious; I would leave the company with whom I walk if I thought it was other than true that they are gathered together unto His name, and that He can say, “there am I in the midst of them”. You will have troubles; would you expect otherwise in the testimony? If you are going through enemy territory do you expect to be unmolested, undisturbed? Do you expect that if something precious of Christ is being formed amongst the saints Satan will not attack it? Of course he will; but I believe that what is essential for all of us to realize is this, “there am I in the midst of them”.

Now that gives the heart strength, and comfort, it also gives the heart the realization that if He is amongst them they are safe and will have guidance in what I have referred to as the pathless desert. Apart from His presence, dear brethren, saints must of necessity be lost in the wilderness; it has happened, alas, to many of God’s people. To try to pick your own way through the desert is an impossibility; you must have the presence of the Lord and the presence of the Spirit if you are to find your way where there is neither track nor signpost, except that which the Lord gives in His grace as present with us. Now may the Lord exercise us about this. I suppose I am quoting another when I say, if you have no exercise, then it is a poor look-out for you. Is everybody here exercised to realize the presence of the Lord and not just to take it for granted? You come to the meetings; you may come because you must come; perhaps father says you must come, and you are too

young to resist. You may come in later years in respect for your father or your mother; but what I would desire is that, as coming, the Lord would give you some sense of His presence, and if you have the sense of His presence I think you would want to come again.

Maybe if the dear brethren in many places who are sitting at home doing nothing, supposedly thinking that everything has gone (which, incidentally, is a reflection on the Lord Himself), came amongst those where the Lord’s presence is known they would get a touch that would quicken their affections towards Him, and get some impression that the Lord is there. I believe others have said that it is as persons come amongst the saints where the Lord’s presence is realized that that really moves them and helps them, and they outgrow the system in which they may be. You say, We do not see much of it; but we see something. We see perhaps one or two green shoots, a little hair growing here and there, one or two added.
Where the ones and twos are added it is surprising how quickly a company can grow.

I think I am right in saying that in the Glanton division one company was reduced to very few persons. And yet through God’s work and through the ministry that the Lord gave (I suppose primarily through our brother Mr. Taylor) they increased again in number. There were subsequent sad divisions, but even now in God’s mercy that company numbers something like eighty persons. We see that, where the Lord’s presence is known, where the Holy Spirit can work unhinderedly, and where the brethren are acting on the principles laid down in Scripture, one by one God can increase assemblies not only spiritually but numerically. We would desire that, but whether we shall see it

is in His hand. What we are seeing we are thankful for, but my concern is this—and I say with frankness and truth it is my concern for myself—that I might not only have the faith of His presence, but the consciousness of it, and that I should be exercised to have suitable conditions in myself so that His presence might be known.

Now we read in John 14, “He that has my commandments and keeps them, he it is that loves me; but he that loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him”. Now I am sure that most of us here would have thought about that expression, “will manifest myself to him”. You will, I am sure, appreciate my quoting what I heard Mr. Taylor say in Croydon. Someone said to him that this would be at the Supper, to which he replied. Well, I would prefer to leave the scripture as it stands, “I ... will manifest myself to him”. In other words his exercise was that, while without any doubt it would be appreciated at the Supper in a very full way, you must leave the Lord free to manifest Himself to any individual anywhere who keeps His commandments. As coming up to the Supper, dear brethren, I believe we should be concerned not to come up formally; not arise from our beds, if I may be very practical, at the latest possible moment and get there on time and then perhaps be preparing throughout the meeting. I think we should be exercised to come together in faith’s anticipation of the Lord manifesting Himself to us, and if we did I believe we should not only speak of these things, as we rightly do, but we should realize them. As I said before, if I think of the presence of the Lord objectively I can only think of it as ecstasy.
Nothing can I think of that could be greater than the consciousness of the presence of the Lord.

and it is that that gives the quickening touch for the service of God; and again, as another has said, if there is no quickening there is no service of God because there is no life. You will have the formula and the order, the right hymns and maybe the right thanksgivings, but if there is no quickening then there is no service of God. The quickening, when everything bursts into life, is when the brethren are conscious that the Lord has come in. May we be exercised about it so that we may understand that christianity is real; it is not a teaching simply, it is not philosophy, as one has said before, I find I have been largely in my life a christian philosopher, and not a very good one at that. But one is beginning to realize that what the Lord is looking for is reality—and one of the last addresses Mr. Raven gave was on

‘Appearances or Realities?’ (‘Ministry of F. E. Raven’, Vol. 19, p.455). May these few thoughts exercise us as to the realization of the presence of the Lord, both as individuals, in our local companies, and generally with those among whom we walk. May it be so for His glory.
We are reminded that the writer of this book, is “the Preacher, the son of David, king in.
Jerusalem” (see Ecclesiastes l: l). There is something unique about the place he has in the canon of Scripture. It speaks in the last chapter about

“The words of the wise … and the collections of them as nails fastened in ... given from one shepherd”. I thought that these three references are a collection of the words of the wise relating to what is under the sun. It is not exactly heavenly light but relates to what is down here. We have to take account of what is down here and as we do so rightly there is profit in it.

So we find in this scripture that things are not to the swift and not to the strong and not to the wise (as far as worldly wisdom and intelligence and knowledge are concerned). Spiritual things do not come that way; this verse would write off that side of things completely. We tend to be taken in by natural ability; we have been taken in by it; it is natural for us to be fond of it. These things appeal to us—the swift, the strong, the intelligent; but divine things do not come that way.

It says, “time and chance”. We cannot say much about chance in spiritual things, but the greatest possible importance is connected with time. God works with time. We are often reminded that God made time and uses time, and according to His own ways in the solving of matters so much depends upon God working, and we have to learn to give time to God to work. As we look back on history we wonder at the way time enters into God’s ways. Forty years in the wilderness; it did not need forty years to extinguish that generation; God could have done it in a day; but God takes time. Then the long time between Malachi and the incoming of Christ, four hundred years, and no scriptural record of anything that took place.

God takes time, uses time. Think of church history in the dark ages, the long period before the recovery; how much God uses time. We cannot help being reminded too about the book of Esther and Esther’s

feast. She invited the king and Haman and they come, and the king says, “What is thy request? even to the half of the kingdom it shall be done”, Esther 5: 6. Esther had everything she needed at that moment, naturally speaking; she had the answer to all her requirements there and then, but she says, “Tomorrow”. We know that that night just gave time for God to work, and what a working took place! So how vital it is that we reckon on God working in His own way and in His own time. Nothing will be perfect unless it comes in that way.

So, to pass on briefly, we have the little city. How valuable our cities are! The divine viewpoint is here spoken of, “a little city”. It enters into the reckoning of this man of skill and divine wisdom, and our cities are meant to be miniatures of the heavenly city. One day all that is being worked out in time, and in God’s ways in time, and His ways with the assembly, and in our local assemblies, is going to take shape in permanency and be displayed in the world to come. All will declare the skill of divine workmanship. These features to be displayed then are to be current, and to be operating. As we think of the wall and the gates, and the street of pure gold (only one street), what features these are to work out in our localities; “In the midst of its street, and of the river, on this side and on that side, the tree of life”, Revelation 22: 2. ‘What delightful features these are, and the enemy is against them.

This “great king” would be against the appearance now of anything that spoke of what God has in mind to display in the city, and so we have the poor wise man who in his wisdom delivered the city. There is the need for wisdom in every city. Job asks, “But wisdom, where shall it be found?” (Job 28: 12). Where is this essential matter that is going to defeat the enemy’s objective and allow

scope for God’s operations city-wise? It is in the city that wisdom is to be found, the wisdom that is of God, which is first pure. James speaks of there being an abundance of it; we have only to ask and the answer to every problem, the answer to every question, is available. The feature of the poor wise man, of course, would be the feature of dependence. There is nothing here of man’s strength; the swift is not here, nor the intelligent and all that kind of thing. We need to covet and develop this feature in our cities and make room for it in whomsoever it may appear. But the poor wise man is not remembered—is despised. That feature does not appeal to the natural sensibilities. It speaks of Christ, of course, and the Spirit of Christ. We need to become appreciative of what God is working with in smallness and in weak conditions to bring about His own great results.
Then there is this other suggestion—“I have seen servants upon horses”. We have seen that, and we do not want to see it again. “The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong”.

Scripture speaks about the driving of Jehu, that he drove furiously; these are not the features we want to develop. It is very attractive to think of “princes walking as servants upon the earth”. The Lord has in mind that princely features should develop amongst us. It says in Psalm 45: 16, “Instead of thy fathers shall be thy sons; princes shalt thou make them in all the earth”. The Lord would dignify the saints in the enjoyment of sonship and bring out features of princeliness. “Walking as servants”; it is not the day for riding upon horses; that day is to come; there are going to be the armies of heaven; we tremble and we sorrow in one sense as we think of it; the day of grace over and the time of judgment, the time of riding on horses, on white horses (see Revelation 19: 14). Now is the time for walking as servants, in all

lowliness, following in the steps of Jesus. “Looking at Jesus as he walked”; John the baptist was enraptured as he saw the Son of God, here in lowly circumstances as a Bondman, walking upon the earth. Paul was minded to go on foot (see Acts 20: 13). May we be encouraged to make way for the development of these features and not be in relation to these other features of the swift and the strong and what is able naturally. May the Lord bless the word.

Satan attacks now through the flesh, so that the young believer begins to learn war ... God would not lead the Israelites by the way of the Philistines because they had not learned war, but now they have got to learn it; they cannot escape doing so. That is a most important thing for young believers—that you cannot escape learning war, but you begin it in yourself ... It is when you get the Spirit that the attack comes. It was after the rock was smitten and the people drank that Amalek attacked. You are already furnished ...

If you had the sense that your body was devoted to Christ, you would be careful how you used it. You would not care to adorn it on the one hand, nor would you be careless about it on the other. If you neglect it, it may become a hindrance; on the other hand, if you indulge your body it will lead to corruption.
